newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bakery firm in poison extortion threat.
newsitem.headline: Australian bakery firm in poison extortion threat.

text.p: Australian supermarket chains began removing Arnotts biscuits (cookies) from their stores on Friday after police confirmed an extortionist had threatened to poison the company's biscuits and plant them in supermarkets.
Share trading in Australia's largest biscuit maker Arnotts was halted on Friday pending an announcement from the company.

An extortion letter and packages containing poisoned biscuits were received by Arnotts, politicians and a media organisation in the states of New South Wales and Queensland on February 3, police said.

The letter demanded that police involved in a murder investigation of a bookmaker in 1991 undergo a lie detector test or poisoned biscuits would be planted in supermarkets along Australia's east coast.

"It's a poison that can kill people...but other poisons can kill you quicker," New South Wales detective chief superintendent Clive Small told a news conference. Small also confirmed Arnotts was the company being threatened.

An Arnotts' spokeswoman told Reuters that Arnotts' chief executive Chris Roberts would not make any comment on the threat until he and police held a press conference. Arnotts is about 70 percent owned by U.S. food processing giant Campbell Soup Co.

The Australian Supermarket Institute said on Friday that Arnotts had asked major retailing chains to remove its entire product range of biscuits and cake mixtures from their shelves in the states of Queensland and New South Wales.

"Our member companies are beginning to take them off the shelves this morning," Institute Associate Director Ken Henrick told Reuters. The Institutes membes include Australia's major supermarket chains Woolworths, Coles Myer, Franklins, Davids and Foodland Associated.
"I think you'll find that every supermarket will have them off their shelves by the same time," said a spokesman for Franklins.
Police were forced to make public the extortion threat on Thursday after media broke an embargo on the threat.

"We believed from the outset that there was no threat to public safety until February 17," Queensland police superintendent Ron Pickering said. "We had appealed to media to keep an embargo while police investigations were carried out."

Police said the extortionist claimed that a man serving a life sentence for the execution-style murder of a bookmaker in 1991 was innocent. The extortion letter said the man was a friend and that the real killers remain free.
"Failing to comply with our demands, a rush of the (foods) will hit stores throughout NSW and Qld," said the extortion letter, part of which was published in The Australian newspaper on Friday.
"This is not a one-off event, it will be a campaign of attacks until this is resolved."
